lines.text: There is no rock on Earth as old as the Earth. The first ones were melted, buried and remade billions of years ago. So how do we know the planet is four and a half billion years old?
The answer came from a rock that fell from the sky — and from a chemist who could not measure it, because everything he touched was poisoned with lead. The air. The water. The dust on his own hands.
To find the age of the Earth, he had to build the cleanest room on the planet. And to explain the lead, he had to take on one of the biggest industries in the world.
He won both fights.
This is how we learned how old the Earth is.
The first scientific answer came in 1862, from the most famous physicist in Britain.

William Thomson — later Lord Kelvin — assumed the Earth had started as a ball of molten rock and had been cooling ever since. Measure how fast heat leaks out of the ground today, and you can run the clock backwards.
His answer: twenty to four hundred million years. Later he narrowed it to twenty to forty. He was wrong by a factor of a hundred — and almost nobody could argue with him.
Geologists hated it. Their layers of rock, their canyons cut grain by grain, seemed to need far longer. Darwin hated it more: twenty million years was nowhere near enough time for evolution.
Others tried different clocks. The Irish physicist John Joly asked how long the rivers would need to carry all the salt that is now in the sea. His answer, in 1899: about ninety million years.
Every clock gave a different answer. And all of them were wrong for the same reason: each assumed a process that had run steadily, and nothing had.

The way out came from somewhere nobody was looking. In 1896, Henri Becquerel found that uranium gives off radiation by itself. Within a few years, Ernest Rutherford showed what that meant: atoms were falling apart.
lines.section: II. A clock inside the rock (2:30–4:00)

lines.text: That broke Kelvin's calculation twice. Radioactive decay heats the Earth from inside, so it cools far more slowly than he assumed. And it gave geologists a new kind of clock.
lines.section: II. A clock inside the rock (2:30–4:00)

lines.text: Uranium decays, through a long chain of steps, into lead, at a rate that never changes — not with heat, not with pressure, not with time. Half of any uranium-238 turns into lead in four and a half billion years.
lines.section: II. A clock inside the rock (2:30–4:00)

lines.text: So if a crystal locked in uranium when it formed, and no lead, then the lead inside it now is a stopwatch. Count the atoms, and you know how long it has been running.
lines.section: II. A clock inside the rock (2:30–4:00)

lines.text: In 1907, the American chemist Bertram Boltwood tried it on real rocks and got ages of up to two billion years. By the 1940s, the oldest rocks pointed to about three billion. The Earth had to be older still — but how much older, no rock on Earth could say.
lines.section: II. A clock inside the rock (2:30–4:00)

lines.text: Remember: no rock on Earth goes back to the beginning. To find the starting line, you need material that formed with the Earth and was never touched again.
Meteorites are exactly that: leftovers from the same cloud that built the planets. In 1948, a young chemist in Chicago named Clair Patterson was given the job of measuring the lead inside them.

It should have taken months. It took seven years. Every time he measured, he found far more lead than could possibly be there. The extra lead was coming from the laboratory itself — from the air, the glassware, the dust, the paint.

So Patterson built one of the first clean rooms in science. Filtered air. Surfaces scrubbed with acid. Chemicals distilled again and again. Anyone entering had to be stripped of lead, down to the dust on their skin.

In 1953, working at Argonne National Laboratory, he finally measured clean lead from a meteorite that had struck Arizona fifty thousand years before. His result: four and a half billion years. Published in 1956: four point five five, give or take seventy million.
Seventy years later, the accepted age is four point five four billion years. His number has barely moved.
But Patterson could not stop thinking about the contamination. Where did all that lead in the air come from?
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: He started measuring lead everywhere — in seawater, in ancient sediments, in layers of ice in Greenland. The pattern was brutal. Old ice held almost none. Recent ice held many times more, and the steepest rise had come in just the last few decades.
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: 1923 was the year tetraethyl lead was first sold as a petrol additive. It stopped engines knocking. And every car on Earth had been spraying lead into the air ever since.
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: In 1965 Patterson published it: the lead in modern people was far above natural levels. The fuel industry pushed back hard. His funding was cut, and he was left off a national committee on lead pollution.
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: He kept going. In 1970 America passed the Clean Air Act, and leaded petrol was phased out over the next twenty-five years. Lead in Americans' blood fell by more than three quarters.
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: The last country on Earth stopped selling leaded petrol for cars in 2021.
lines.section: IV. Where the lead came from (5:40–7:20)

lines.text: Today the oldest pieces of the solar system are dated to four billion five hundred and sixty-seven million years. The oldest crystal found on Earth, a zircon from Western Australia, is four point four billion years old.
And the Earth itself: four point five four billion, give or take about one per cent — read from the lead inside a rock that fell from the sky.
Clair Patterson found the age of the world by learning to see lead. And then he got the lead out of it.
The last digit is still being argued over. The first ones have not moved since 1956.
